3.  Resolution Approving Application for TDA Article 8 Funds
  The City receives, through the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation
  Authority, Transportation Development Act funds from Article 8. Historically these
  funds have been used to fund the City’s public transportation contract. Staff
  proposes to continue the utilization of these funds for the transit system.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution approving the annual application for Transit Development Act
  (TDA) funds for Fiscal Year 2027.

4.  Request for Proposals for Professional Audit Services
  Staff is requesting permission to issue a RFP to qualified certified public accountant firms
  to audit its financial statements for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, with the option
  of auditing its financial statements for each of the two (2) subsequent fiscal years, in
  addition to performing other financial audits and reviews as specified in the RFP.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize City Staff to solicit requests for proposals (RFP) to provide professional auditing
  services for the fiscal years ending June 30, 2026 (FY26), 2027 (FY27), and 2028 (FY28).

5.  Fire Department Mobile Incident Command Conversion Package
  The Avalon Fire Department incident command vehicle needs to be equipped with a
  state-of-the-art mobile communications terminal that allows the battalion chief to receive
  real-time incident information and maintain communications with Avalon Sheriff’s
  dispatch center and other local law enforcement.
  Recommended Action
  1. Per the City’s Procurement Policy, authorize the City Manager or his designee to
  execute an agreement with SilCo Enterprises for the purchase of a Command Vehicle
  Conversion Package for a not-to-exceed sum of $80,000. 2. Amend the Fiscal Year 25-
  26 Budget allocating $100,000 to the Fire Vehicle Replacement Fund, Account # 10245-
  6871, CIP Project Number 234501 to recognize a donation from the Offield Foundation.

6.  Repair and Maintenance of City Shoreboat Float
  The City-owned Shoreboat Float needs routine annual maintenance including the
  removal and installation of new bottom paint, anodes, and repairs to its structure.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize an expenditure of an amount not to exceed $60,000 to Al Larson Boat Shop, a
  sole source vender, for the rehabilitation of the City-owned Shore-boat Float from account
  #10470-5705.

GENERAL BUSINESS

7.  Catalina Xtreme Parasail DBA Catalina Coastal Tours Transportation Permit Application
  On March 13, 2026 David Montano with Catalina Xtreme Parasail DBA Catalina Coastal
  Tours submitted a transportation permit application to provide tours within the City of
  Avalon utilizing a residential autoette permit.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
APRIL 7, 2026
PAGE 3

  Recommended Action
  1. Receive presentation. 2. Discuss. 3. If consensus is met, approve the Transportation
  Permit for Catalina Xtreme Parasail DBA Catalina Coastal Tours, to utilize a Residential
  Autoette vehicle permit to conduct City tours with stated conditions.

8.  Pedicab Catalina Transportation Permit Application
  On February 9, 2026, the City received an application for a Transportation Permit for Joe
  Sampson’s Pedicab Catalina. Mr. Sampson will be utilizing a Broadway Pedicab custom
  built by Main Street Pedicab that provides three-person seating.
  Recommended Action
  1. Receive presentation. 2. Discuss. 3. If consensus is met, approve a Transportation
  Permit for Joe Sampson’s Pedicab Catalina for one pedicab to conduct tours with stated
  conditions. 4. If consensus is met, allow for the operation of the pedicab on Front Street
  between Metropole and Sumner.

9.  Consideration of Short-Term and Long-Term Rental Policy
  Generally, direct incentive programs are the most commonly pursued option by cities for
  incentivizing long-term rentals. The City already has disincentivized short-term rentals in
  its recent update to its short-term rental regulations, though staff continues to monitor
  methods used in other jurisdictions and outcomes from these recent regulations.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss options to incentivize long-term rental within the City and evaluate City long-
  term and short-term rental policies.

ADJOURN

Devin Elise Hart, Senior Management Analyst

GENERAL BUSINESS

9.  2025 General Plan Housing Element Annual Progress Report
  City Council received and filed the General Plan Housing Element Annual Report for 2025
  and directed staff to submit the Housing Element Annual Progress Report to the California
  Department of Housing and Community Development and the Governor’s Office of Land
  Use and Climate Innovation.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Michael Ponce.
  (4 Ayes-Marshall, De La Rosa, Lavelle and Ponce; 1 Absent-Schickling)

10.  Electric Vessel Charging Infrastructure at Avalon Harbor
  1. City Council made an affirmative finding to dispense with a competitive procurement
  process due to economic efficiency as outlined in Avalon Municipal Code 3-4.111(c). 2.
  Authorized the City Manager to negotiate the purchase and installation of a marine
  electric vessel charger with Aqua superPower.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Yesenia De La Rosa.
  (4 Ayes-Marshall, De La Rosa, Lavelle and Ponce; 1 Absent-Schickling)

11.  Civic Center Housing Project Phase 3A Bid Results
  Pursuant to Public Contract Code Section 20167: 1. City Council rejected all bids
  received for the Civic Center Housing Phase 3A: Site Preparation Project; 2. Adopted
  Resolution No. 26-1 1 of the City Council of the City of Avalon Rejecting All Bids
  Received for the Civic Center Housing Project Phase 3A: Site Preparation and
  Authorization to Negotiate. 3. Authorized the City Manager or designee to negotiate a
  revised contract scope with Jordahl Construction, Inc. for the Civic Center Housing
  Project Phase 3A: Site Preparation and return to City Council for final award.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Michael Ponce.
  (4 Ayes-Marshall, De La Rosa, Lavelle and Ponce; 1 Absent-Schickling)

12.  Setting a Public Hearing Date for the Proposed Rate Changes to the Sewer, Salt Water,
  and Solid Waste Service Fees
  1. City Council discussed and provided direction to Staff regarding the fees for the Sewer,
  Saltwater, and Solid Waste services. These property-related fees can only be increased
  by a four-fifths vote of the City Council. 2. City Council set a public hearing for May 19,
  2026 for the City Council to hear public comments on the annual sewer, saltwater, and
  solid waste fees.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Yesenia De La Rosa.
  (4 Ayes-Marshall, De La Rosa, Lavelle and Ponce; 1 Absent-Schickling)

13.  Advance Payment of Measure C Funds to the Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC)
  City Council provided direction on whether to enter into the letter of interest which could
  lead to an agreement wherein the City advances approximately $2,927,441.90 for CIMC’s
  participation in the Voluntary Rate Range Intergovernmental Transfer Program, which
  CIMC believes will result in increased funding for CIMC. The City would be paid back
  through any available CIMC revenues, including Measure C funds, over the course of
  several years.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Lisa Lavelle.
  (4 Ayes-Marshall, De La Rosa, Lavelle and Ponce; 1 Absent-Schickling)

  The City of Avalon is a tourism-driven, harbor community located on Santa

Council-Manager form of government. Policy-making and legislative authority are
vested in the City Council, consisting of the mayor and four council members, all
of whom are elected at large. The Mayor is elected for a two-year term and council

implementing policies and ordinances approved by the City Council and

the City Attorney and City Clerk.

protection, planning and zoning, building inspections, recreation and other
community services, and the maintenance and improvements of streets and other
infrastructure. The City is also responsible for various enterprise funds providing

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize an expenditure of an amount not to exceed $60,000
to Al Larson Boat Shop, a sole source vender, for the rehabilitation of the City-owned Shore-
boat Float from account #10470-5705.

REPORT SUMMARY: On October 7, 2025 the City Council authorized the purchase of the
Shoreboat Float and amended account #10470-5705 adding an additional $60,000 for annual
maintenance of the float.

The City-owned Shoreboat Float needs routine annual maintenance including the removal and
installation of new bottom paint, anodes, and repairs to its structure.

On December 17, 2019, the City Council designated Al Larson Boat Shop as a sole source
vendor, as defined in the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.111(b), to contract for repair and
maintenance on certain City-owned floats.

Al Larson Boat Shop uses a unique rail system for hauling floats and vessels out of the water.
The vessel, or float, is “floated” onto a platform, blocked and secured, and then the entire
platform is winched up the rails to its final dry dock position. This is the safest, most efficient
and cost-effective way to haul the City’s floats out of the water, thus satisfying the sole source
requirements.

City Staff recommends the City Council authorizes an expenditure not-to-exceed $60,000 to Al
Larson Boat Shop, a sole source vender, for the rehabilitation of the City-owned Shore-boat
Float from account #10470-5705.

the Fiscal Year 2025-26 Budget.

SUBJECT:  Consideration of Short-Term and Long-Term Rental Policy

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Discuss options to incentivize long-term rental within the City
and evaluate City long-term and short-term rental policies.

REPORT SUMMARY: Generally, direct incentive programs are the most commonly pursued
option by cities for incentivizing long-term rentals. The City already has disincentivized short-
term rentals in its recent update to its short-term rental regulations, though staff continues to
monitor methods used in other jurisdictions and outcomes from these recent regulations.

BACKGROUND: Avalon experiences unique challenges in providing for affordable housing.
Unlike neighboring landlocked cities, Avalon is on an island, surrounded on all sides by water or
land used for natural preservation. This means that there are limited opportunities to increase
housing production. Even where those opportunities exist, the City has a limited supply of water
that must be confirmed available before a project is approved. Compounding Avalon’s
geographical and practical constraints to developing new housing, it is also a popular destination
for tourists who appreciate Avalon’s unique character and natural beauty. The demand for short-
term rentals in the City can make converting housing stock to transient rental a lucrative
opportunity.

The City has enacted regulations on short-term rentals intended to help preserve long-term
housing stock. However, long-term rental incentives may also cause property owners to consider
making their properties available for long-term rent. Many community members have submitted
public comment expressing an increasing inability to afford living on the island. Workforce
housing projects can contribute to reducing housing costs for workers that are essential to
supporting Avalon’s vibrant commercial businesses, schools, and other critical services.

Residents express a desire for additional long-term housing availability. Residents also express
a desire to use their primary residences for short term rental as a means of increased financial
security. Balancing these objectives requires a nuanced regulatory approach. Staff has
evaluated the suggestions made by the public and used by other cities, in light of California
constitutional constraints, landlord-tenant law, and programs used in comparable resort and
coastal jurisdictions.

DISCUSSION: Comparable jurisdictions include the resort communities of the Town of Truckee,
Town of Mammoth Lakes, and City of South Lake Tahoe. These jurisdictions use cash incentives

 (City grants) to convert vacant or short-term rented units to leases lasting several or more
months, most commonly twelve months. South Lake Tahoe ties payments to successful lease
completion and imposes a maximum rent ceiling to align subsidy dollars with affordability goals.
These models are especially relevant because they were designed for tourism economies with
intense seasonable pressure on local housing supply, like Avalon.

Other jurisdictions, like the cities of San Francisco and Pasadena, have sustainable short term
rental policies. These cities provide local property owners with the ability to supplement their
income sources with short-term rentals, but limit this opportunity to those who reside in the cities
for a given length of time. Property owners must live in the property where a unit is rented for at
least nine months out of the year. The maximum number of days a property owner can rent out
a unit for short term rental is 90 days out of the year. Similarly, Los Angeles caps unhosted stays
at 120 days of the calendar year. These limitations on short term rentals can accomplish the
goal of allowing residents to supplement their income with their properties while not completely
eliminating those rentals from the housing market for the entirety of the year.

The City’s current Transient Rental License Ordinance may unintentionally discourage the
retention and re-establishment of long-term rentals. The code provides that a property owner is
ineligible for a transient rental license if the unit has been rented for a consecutive 30 day period
at any point in the two years preceding the application. Specifically, the code directs that a
Transient Rental License application “should be denied” in this circumstance. The rule was
adopted before the current cap on short term rentals to prevent the conversion of long-term
rentals to short-term rentals, but some have raised concerns regarding the outcomes of the rule.
As reflected in public comment, property owners who maintain tenants at stays of 30 consecutive
days or more are effectively incentivized to keep their units off the market for two years. This
incentive may be possible for owners who can afford this loss of rental income for two years, but
may be economically infeasible for other owners who rely on the rental income. As a result,
owners who continue to rent to local residents may foreclose their future eligibility for a transient
rental license, while owners who remove tenants or leave units vacant may preserve that option.
Public comment indicates this creates a perverse incentive structure in which long-term tenants
are displaced and units are taken offline in anticipation of future transient rental eligibility, rather
than encouraging the continued provision of year-round housing. One mechanism could be
giving property owners that provide long-term rentals a kind of short-term rental credit (e.g. an
allotted number of days where short term rental is permitted) or this provision could be
eliminated.

Public comment received by staff has suggested other novel options not yet pursued in other
jurisdictions. One suggestion was to reduce utility fees for year-round rentals. Under the
California Constitution, a fee may not exceed the estimated reasonable cost of the service. As
a result, there would need to be a basis in cost-of-service to suggest those fees could be validly
reduced and one class of users should be treated differently than others. Due to the legal
limitations on how fees may be imposed on property owners, this approach would require legal
evaluation and may be unworkable. Similarly, property taxes are imposed by the County tax
assessor and the City does not control those tax rates, meaning the City lacks authority to
regulate in that area. This is why cities have instead opted for incentives provided through their
general funds.

 The use of general fund dollars would need to be supported by public purpose justifications.
Under the California Constitution, it is impermissible to provide public funds without a
corresponding public benefit. A well-designed housing incentive program can satisfy that
standard if payments are tied to public objectives such as increased workforce housing supply
and improved availability of affordable housing. Like the programs used in the jurisdictions
above, any incentive payment should require a written agreement supporting that the housing
unit will be used for long-term rental prior to payment.

Incentivizing long-term rentals has primarily relied on a grant-based mechanism in a majority of
cities. The effectiveness of these grants will depend on the relative economic benefits of short
term renting. Meanwhile, the City has recently regulated in the area of short term rentals,
particularly imposing more stringent requirements on operators and a cap on licenses. The
effects of those changes are at the beginning stages, though staff continues to monitor,
particularly once the transient rental license cap is met. If Council chooses to move forward with
incentives for long-term rentals, staff will return with suggested options for an incentive program
based on Council’s discussion and direction and public comment.
